segments.text: In 1902, Hanoi was expanding its infrastructure, but the city quickly ran into a major problem
in its newly built sewers—rats.
There were thousands of them swarming through the wet underground brick tunnels, creating
a severe public health hazard.
City officials devised what they thought was a highly efficient solution.
They introduced a bounty system that paid cash to anyone who turned in a rat's tail.
The logic seemed airtight.
A severed tail was hard proof of a kill, meaning every tail collected equated to exactly one
less passed in the sewers.
Initially, the program appeared to be a massive success.
Hunters flooded government offices, dropping off thousands of tails and collecting their
reward money.
Then, residents noticed a strange anomaly above ground.
Rats were running through the streets, perfectly healthy, but completely missing their tails.
The rat hunters had realized that a dead rat pays out exactly once, but a live rat can
breed.
They were catching the rats, clipping the tails for cash, and releasing the animals
back into the city to create a continuous supply of inventory.
Some enterprising locals even started covert rat breeding farms.
When the city finally canceled the program, officials were left staring at a mountain
of tails, and the city had more rats than when the bounty started.
The financial incentive, designed to eliminate the pests, actually multiplied them.
A logical plan on paper broke down the moment it interacted with human behavior.
This infographic outlines four case studies where we can directly compare what creators
expected to happen with what actually occurred in reality.
Look at early SMS technology.
Mobile networks originally built it as a highly restricted, one-way system to broadcast
short administrative updates to subscribers.
Young cell phone users figured out how to use the tech to message each other, turning
a basic network tool into an essential method of daily two-way communication.
Similarly, the military designed the global positioning system, specifically to pinpoint
locations and navigate units around the globe.
While it excels at navigation, the system's precise satellite clocks are now the invisible
infrastructure required to synchronize global banking transactions, keep power grids running,
and coordinate millions of gig economy deliveries.
The most valuable applications of these digital tools emerged well after the initial
blueprints were drawn.
We see similar forecasting failures when we intervene in physical environments.
In the 1930s, Australia imported cane toads to eat the beetles that were
destroying their sugar cane crops.
The toads almost completely ignored the beetles.
Instead, they poisoned native predators that tried to eat them and multiplied rapidly,
spreading across the continent as a destructive, invasive species.
Urban planners run into the exact same issue.
Houston officials spent $2.8 billion to widen the Katy freeway, a massive project
designed specifically to ease daily traffic congestion.
Between 2011 and 2014, rush hour trips on the widened highway actually grew 30 to 55%
longer, adding more lanes simply encouraged more people to drive.
Biological ecosystems and concrete highways are intricate networks.
Pulling a single lever to fix a localized issue usually triggers compounding reactions
across the entire system.
Whether it's pest control, telecommunications, or traffic management,
our track record is remarkably consistent.
We routinely fail to predict the ultimate outcomes of our interventions,
which brings us to the current, intense societal debate surrounding artificial
intelligence.
This chart visualizes the current predictions.
You have optimists drawing a path upward to utopian efficiency,
and warriors plotting a downward line toward economic collapse.
If history is any guide, the actual path of reality will diverge entirely.
No researcher, tech CEO, or government regulator knows exactly where this
technology is going to land.
It is highly likely that the most significant effect AI will have on
your daily life is an application, or a complication, that no one in any lab
has even thought of yet.
Some of the biggest results are the ones nobody predicted.
That unpredictability gives us a reason to keep paying attention,
and it's the best reason to stay curious.
